name: Dance (social and recreational dance and dance movement therapy)
origin: People have danced in healing rituals since early human history, and dance became a formal therapy in the United States from the 1940s and 1950s through the work of dancer Marian Chace, whose classes drew patients referred by doctors and led to work at Saint Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, D.C.; she became the first president of the American Dance Therapy Association when it was founded in 1966.
summary: This point covers dancing for mental health and wellbeing, from social, partner and recreational dance classes in any style to dance movement therapy (DMT). The American Dance Therapy Association defines DMT as the psychotherapeutic use of movement to promote emotional, social, cognitive and physical integration of the individual, for the purpose of improving health and well-being, and it is delivered by a trained therapist, often in groups. Recreational dance is taught by dancers or exercise instructors and aims at enjoyment, fitness and skill, though studies suggest it can also ease low mood and anxiety.
theoryOfChange: Dance is physical exercise, so it may help mood through the same routes as other exercise; in a large review of exercise for depression, the benefit grew with the intensity prescribed. Dance also adds music, learning and moving in time with other people: in an experiment with 94 adults, small groups who danced in sync to music for 13 minutes felt closer to each other and showed higher pain thresholds, a rough sign of endorphin release, than groups who moved out of sync. In dance movement therapy, movement is also treated as a way to express and work through feelings that are hard to put into words, and mirroring another person's movements is used to build a felt, physical relationship; these are proposed mechanisms, not proven ones.
whatYouDo: In a dance class you learn steps or routines in a style such as salsa, tango, ballroom, folk or contemporary dance, usually in a group and often with a partner, set to music. In dance movement therapy, a trained therapist leads a warm-up and then structured improvisation, mirroring and creative movement, sometimes with props such as scarves or balls and music you help choose, and the session ends by talking about what came up; group work in the style of Marian Chace and Authentic Movement, where one person moves with eyes closed while another witnesses, are common approaches. Many people also dance on their own at home, at social dances or in clubs.
typicalDose: In a 2019 meta-analysis of dance and dance movement therapy studies, programs lasted about 11 weeks on average (from 1 to 32 weeks), usually with about two sessions a week of 40 to 120 minutes (about 70 minutes on average). In dance movement therapy trials for adult depression, people attended 12 to 36 sessions, 1 to 5 times a week, each lasting 45 to 120 minutes; recreational dancers set their own dose, from a weekly class to regular social dancing.
keyTechniques: Learning steps and routines in styles such as salsa, tango, folk or ballroom
Partner and group dancing in time with music
Group circle work in the Chace style and Authentic Movement
Talking about the feelings that came up while moving

evidence.summary: Several meta-analyses point to benefits for mood, but most studies are small and at risk of bias. A 2019 meta-analysis of 41 controlled studies with 2,374 people found medium improvements overall, including for depression (18 studies) and anxiety (9 studies), with small but consistent effects for dance movement therapy and larger but less consistent ones for dance classes, and the authors note that observer-rated outcomes gave bigger effects, possibly a sign of bias (Koch and colleagues, 2019). For adults with depression, a 2019 review found a large benefit when dance movement therapy was added to usual care in the 3 trials at moderate to low risk of bias (111 adults; Karkou and colleagues), whereas an earlier Cochrane review of 3 small trials with 147 people judged the evidence too weak for firm conclusions (Meekums and colleagues, 2015). In a 2024 network meta-analysis of exercise for major depression, dance showed the largest drop in symptoms of any exercise type but rested on only 107 people, mostly young women, with very low confidence in the result (Noetel and colleagues), and a 2024 review of 27 studies found structured dance about as effective as other structured exercise for anxiety and depressive symptoms (Fong Yan and colleagues).

goodFitFor: People who enjoy music and moving and would find dancing more fun than other exercise, who want mood and fitness benefits with built-in social contact, or who find feelings easier to express through the body than in words. Dance movement therapy suits people who want professional support for depression, anxiety or other conditions alongside their usual care.
cautions: Dance carries the ordinary risks of exercise, such as sprains, falls and overuse injuries, so start at a level that fits your fitness, check with a doctor first if you have heart, joint or balance problems, and pick styles and partners that respect your comfort with touch. Expressive work in dance movement therapy can bring up strong feelings or memories, and in care-home dance sessions some residents with dementia showed confusion, irritability or anxiety, so trauma survivors and other vulnerable people are best served by a credentialed therapist (R-DMT or BC-DMT in the United States). Dance is an add-on to professional treatment for serious depression or other mental illness, not a replacement for it.
namingNote: Named Dance and defined broadly, as requested: social, partner and recreational dance of any style (classes, dance fitness, social dances or dancing at home) plus dance movement therapy, which is called dance/movement therapy in the United States and dance movement psychotherapy in the United Kingdom; DMT here always means the therapy, not the drug with the same initials. The family is arts rather than movement because dance is an expressive art led by music and dance movement therapy is one of the creative arts therapies, which sets this point apart from the exercise points (HIIT, team sport, endurance training, strength training and Qigong), though its exercise side shows up in the evidence. Research separates dance movement therapy, led by a trained therapist within a therapeutic relationship, from dance interventions taught by dancers or exercise instructors, and the evidence summary labels each finding accordingly.
